title: Unsteady With Absent Ankle Jerks / Nitrous Oxide Can Cause Functional B12 Deficiency

blocks.text: Unsteady With Absent Ankle Jerks / Nitrous Oxide Can Cause Functional B12 Deficiency

Code R5-121 · Physical examination · PACES Station 3, neurological examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 minutes (up to 6 examining; at least 4 questioning) · UK hospital outpatient setting · Source dates listed in §15 · AMaC examiner-style educational station; not an official PACES marking scheme.
Please examine this patient’s lower limbs to establish the cause of their unsteadiness. Present your findings and answer the examiners’ questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. Absent ankle reflexes do not rule out spinal cord disease when the plantar responses are extensor. Combined posterior column and corticospinal signs point to subacute combined degeneration.

The Examiner Trap. Mistaking this for isolated peripheral neuropathy or reassuring on a normal serum B12 is unsafe. Nitrous oxide can cause functional B12 inactivation; do not delay treatment in a patient with neurological signs.

blocks.text: Not applicable — this is an examination encounter with a patient, not a communication or consultation role-player. The patient may answer brief, natural questions but is not a surrogate.
Patient setup: A 24-year-old who reports difficulty walking in the dark and frequent falls.
Finding-release protocol: do not announce a sign before the corresponding manoeuvre is performed.
Lower-limb power mildly reduced, particularly distally; ankle jerks absent; knee jerks preserved.
Extensor plantar responses; impaired vibration and joint position sense at toes; positive Romberg sign and a stamping sensory ataxic gait.
Pinprick is less affected than proprioception; no clear cerebellar limb dysmetria.
Normal-findings variant: If strength is normal, state it accurately: sensory ataxia can occur with preserved power.
Examiner question ladder (4–6 questions; 4-minute discussion):
Q1 [R2]: Where is the lesion?  Model: Posterior columns plus corticospinal tracts of the cord, with possible peripheral nerve involvement.
Q2 [R3]: Why absent ankle jerks and upgoing toes?  Model: Coexisting peripheral neuropathy and spinal cord tract disease.
Q3 [R4]: Can B12 be normal?  Model: Yes, functional deficiency from nitrous oxide may not be apparent from total serum B12; use MMA or homocysteine.
Q4 [R5]: What do you do now?  Model: Take appropriate samples and begin B12 replacement without waiting for results, stop nitrous oxide and assess safety.
Q5 [R6]: What else needs exclusion?  Model: Cord compression, inflammatory myelopathy, copper deficiency and other nutritional causes.

Curveball: The candidate states a diagnosis with certainty before discussing alternatives. Safe response: “These are findings and a leading differential; confirmation needs the appropriate investigation.”
[R1; Skill A] Test tone, power, knee and ankle reflexes, plantars, proprioception and gait.
[R2; Skill B] Identify absent ankle jerks, extensor plantars and sensory ataxia.
[R3; Skill D] Recognise probable subacute combined degeneration.
[R4; Skill E] Seek nitrous oxide exposure, check MMA or homocysteine and investigate other causes.
[R5; Skill E] Start B12 replacement promptly, arrange neurology review and cease nitrous oxide.
[R6; Skill G] Ask about falls, use assistance for gait and avoid shaming substance use.
[G] Gains consent, checks discomfort, and protects dignity during examination.

CANDIDATE: “Hello. I would like to examine you to help work out what is going on. Is that okay? Tell me if anything is painful.” [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: “Test tone, power, knee and ankle reflexes, plantars, proprioception and gait. I will do this systematically and help you if you are unsteady.” [R1 Pass]
EXAMINER: “Summarise the key examination findings.”

CANDIDATE: “Lower-limb power mildly reduced, particularly distally; ankle jerks absent; knee jerks preserved. Extensor plantar responses; impaired vibration and joint position sense at toes; positive Romberg sign and a stamping sensory ataxic gait.” [R2 Pass]
EXAMINER: “What is your impression?”
CANDIDATE: “Posterior columns plus corticospinal tracts of the cord, with possible peripheral nerve involvement. I would also consider relevant alternatives.” [R3 Pass]
EXAMINER: “What would you do next?”
CANDIDATE: “Seek nitrous oxide exposure, check MMA or homocysteine and investigate other causes. Start B12 replacement promptly, arrange neurology review and cease nitrous oxide.” [R4 Pass; R5 Pass]
Examiner note: Demonstrates a safe, adequately justified assessment and explicit welfare action.
High-performance performance (adds prioritisation and anticipatory reasoning).
CANDIDATE: “Before examining, I will check whether any manoeuvre worsens pain or threatens balance and maintain your privacy.” [R6 High-performance]
CANDIDATE: “Test sensory pathways carefully and support the patient during Romberg.” [R1 High-performance]
EXAMINER: “Which signs are discriminating?”
CANDIDATE: “Localise both posterior column and corticospinal tract dysfunction. I will state clearly what I did not find.” [R2 High-performance]
EXAMINER: “What else could explain them?”
CANDIDATE: “Distinguish B12 deficiency, copper deficiency and compressive myelopathy.” [R3 High-performance]
EXAMINER: “How does that change your plan?”
CANDIDATE: “Arrange MRI if needed to exclude compressive or inflammatory myelopathy; address falls, rehabilitation and substance-use support.” [R4 High-performance; R5 High-performance]
CANDIDATE: “I will document function and arrange appropriate assistance before the patient leaves.” [R6 High-performance]
Examiner note: Uses objective localisation, offers proportionate investigations, anticipates welfare concerns and avoids unjustified certainty.
R1 — Directed limb and gait examination: Failing to test tone, power, knee and ankle reflexes, plantars, proprioception and gait makes the assessment less safe or less discriminating.
R2 — Mixed cord and peripheral signs: Failing to identify absent ankle jerks, extensor plantars and sensory ataxia makes the assessment less safe or less discriminating.
R3 — Neurological localisation: Failing to recognise probable subacute combined degeneration makes the assessment less safe or less discriminating.
R4 — Investigation: Failing to seek nitrous oxide exposure, check MMA or homocysteine and investigate other causes makes the assessment less safe or less discriminating.
“Absent ankles alone are misleading: the upgoing plantars localise a central tract problem.”
“I would treat suspected neurological B12 deficiency promptly, not wait for a number.”
Absent ankle reflexes do not rule out spinal cord disease when the plantar responses are extensor. Combined posterior column and corticospinal signs point to subacute combined degeneration.

Mistaking this for isolated peripheral neuropathy or reassuring on a normal serum B12 is unsafe. Nitrous oxide can cause functional B12 inactivation; do not delay treatment in a patient with neurological signs.
Take appropriate samples and begin B12 replacement without waiting for results, stop nitrous oxide and assess safety.
THINK: progressive myelopathy and falls.
SAY: “Mixed posterior column and upper motor neurone signs.”
DO: check joint position, plantars and gait safely.
NUMBERS: NICE NG239 (2024) supports MMA or homocysteine for nitrous oxide exposure.
TRAP: a normal total B12 falsely reassures.
FINISH: prompt replacement, stop exposure, neurology and rehabilitation.

NICE NG239 (2024), recommendations — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng239/chapter/Recommendations — Supports: Nitrous oxide functional B12 deficiency: MMA or homocysteine, prompt replacement. Access checked 13 October 2026.
Educational use only. No automatic claim of examination scoring or independent clinical sign-off.

Check nitrous oxide exposure specifically; serum B12 can be normal despite functional inactivation. Evaluate cord and peripheral nerve deficits and alternative causes. Advise complete cessation and initiate appropriate B12 replacement without delaying treatment in a neurologically symptomatic patient. NICE NG239 recommends oral or intramuscular B12 for nitrous-oxide-related B12 deficiency according to clinical judgement; in a patient with significant neurological injury, obtain urgent specialist input on parenteral treatment and follow-up.
